Hugging Face Embedding Engine

Source: R/sentence_embeddings-huggingface.R
embedding_huggingface.Rd

embedding_huggingface() creates an engine for step_sentence_embeddings() that runs a sentence-transformers model from the Hugging Face Hub on your own machine, using Python through reticulate.

Usage

embedding_huggingface(
  model,
  revision,
  device = NULL,
  text_prefix = NULL,
  normalize = FALSE,
  batch_size = 32
)

Arguments

model

A single string giving the id of the model on the Hugging Face Hub, such as "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2". There is no default, so the model is always visible in your code.

revision

A single string giving the version of the model to use, preferably the hash of a commit. A branch name such as "main" is accepted, but it can point to a different version later on, which defeats the purpose of pinning. See the details for how to find the hash. There is no default, so the version is always visible in your code.

device

A single string giving the device to run the model on: "cpu", "cuda", "mps", or a numbered device such as "cuda:1". Defaults to NULL, which lets sentence-transformers choose a device. The choice then depends on the machine, so set it if you want the recipe to behave in the same way everywhere.

text_prefix

A single string added to the start of every text before it is embedded, or NULL for no prefix. Some models are trained with prefixes, for example "query: " or "passage: " for the e5 models. Defaults to NULL.

normalize

A single logical. If TRUE, each embedding is scaled to have unit length. Defaults to FALSE, which returns the vectors as the model returns them. Some models already return vectors of unit length.

batch_size

A single positive whole number giving the maximum number of texts the model embeds at once. Larger batches are faster, up to the memory of the device. Defaults to 32.

Value

An object of class sentence_embedding_engine.

Details

The embeddings are what SentenceTransformer$encode() returns for the model, so the pooling and normalization steps that are part of the model are used. Texts longer than the maximum sequence length of the model are cut off by the model, as they are in sentence-transformers.

The model is downloaded from the Hub the first time it is used, and is kept in the Hugging Face cache on your machine, which is usually ~/.cache/huggingface. After that the model runs locally, and your text is not sent anywhere. Loading a model into memory takes a while, so the loaded model is kept for the rest of the R session. Each parallel worker loads its own copy.

The engine stores the model id, the revision, and the other settings, not the model. A prepped recipe therefore needs the Python environment and the model at the same revision to be available where it is baked. They are downloaded on first use if the machine can reach the Hub.

Before any text is embedded, the engine checks that the Python module can be imported, that the device is available, and that the model can be loaded at the revision, and gives an error that says what is wrong if not.

Requires the reticulate package and the Python module sentence_transformers. Models that need trust_remote_code are not supported.

Pinning the revision

A model repository on the Hub can be updated, so the same model id can give different embeddings over time. The revision argument fixes the version. To find the hash of the latest commit, open the model page and then Files and versions, or request https://huggingface.co/api/models/<model> and read the sha field. Models that are pinned to a commit give the same embeddings every time, up to small differences between devices.

Setting up Python

The engine needs the Python module sentence_transformers, which brings in torch. If you don't already have a Python environment you want to use, either of these works:

  • Install it into the environment reticulate uses, for example with reticulate::py_install("sentence-transformers").

  • Before Python is started in the R session, run reticulate::py_require("sentence-transformers"), and reticulate sets up a temporary environment for you.

See the reticulate documentation for choosing an environment.

macOS

On macOS, loading torch in an R session that already has some R packages loaded, such as data.table (which recipes depends on), can abort R with the error OMP: Error #15: Initializing libomp.dylib, but found libomp.dylib already initialized. This happens because both load their own OpenMP library. To avoid it, the engine sets the environment variables KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK to "TRUE" and OMP_NUM_THREADS to "1" before the model is loaded, unless you have already set them, and tells you when it does. The model then runs on one thread, which is slower. The OpenMP developers describe KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK as an unsafe workaround that can in principle give wrong results. In testing, the embeddings matched those of Python to within 1e-6. Set both variables yourself, for example in .Renviron, to use other values or to stop the engine from setting them.

The variables only help if they are set before Python is started. If you have already used reticulate to start Python in the R session, for example with reticulate::py_config(), the engine is too late to prevent the crash. Restart R and set the variables in .Renviron in that case.

See also

step_sentence_embeddings()

Other Embedding Engines: embedding_custom(), embedding_ollama()

Examples

if (FALSE) {
# Needs Python with the sentence-transformers module, and downloads the model
library(recipes)

sample_data <- tibble(
  text = c("The cat sat.", "A dog ran.", "Stocks fell sharply today.")
)

rec <- recipe(~text, data = sample_data) |>
  step_sentence_embeddings(
    text,
    engine = embedding_huggingface(
      "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
      revision = "1110a243fdf4706b3f48f1d95db1a4f5529b4d41",
      device = "cpu"
    )
  )

rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)
}
